claims.claim: REMOVED, the sweep's Q-FAIL on this page and independently re-confirmed by fresh grep of the stored notice: "copper-nickel sulfide mining in the area would use water-intensive processes that, BLM determined, posed an unacceptable risk of acid mine drainage into the watershed." Public Land Order 7917 makes no such determination. It never uses the words "acid", "acidity", "water quality", "water-intensive" or "sulfide" at all; its stated purposes are ecological integrity and wilderness values in the Rainy River Watershed, the BWCAW, the Mining Protection Area and the 1854 Ceded Territory, plus the health, traditional cultural values and subsistence-based lifestyle of the Tribes. The sentence attributed a specific technical finding to a named federal agency in a document that does not contain it - the same fabricated-attribution family as the four fabrications struck on 2026-08-30. FIXED BY SOURCING, not by softening: the water-quality reasoning does exist, in the Forest Service's withdrawal APPLICATION notice at 86 FR 58299, and the page now quotes it there, in its own words ("threatened by potential future sulfide mining"; "effluent with elevated levels of acidity, metals, and other potential contaminants"; "irreversible degradation of this key water-based wilderness resource"), and says in terms that it is not in the order. CORRECTIONS-BORDERLINE, FLAGGED FOR JAMES, NOT LOGGED: this is deferred candidate #3 in HANDOFF-AUDIT-SWEEP-PHASE-B.md section 5 D1, and section 9.1 D1 defers all corrections entries.

REMOVED, F-FAIL, two instances of one error: "withdrew 225,504 acres of National Forest land from mineral entry and geothermal leasing" and "the 225,504 acres reverts to its prior status under the Mining Law of 1872 and applicable National Forest rules". Mineral entry is the location system of the General Mining Law of 1872; the order withdraws only "from disposition under the United States mineral and geothermal leasing laws" and names the Mineral Leasing Act of 1920, the Geothermal Steam Act of 1970, the Mineral Leasing Act for Acquired Lands of 1947, section 402 of Reorganization Plan No. 3 of 1946, 16 U.S.C. 520 and 16 U.S.C. 508b. Confirmed by exhaustive search: neither "mineral entry" nor "1872" nor "General Mining Law" occurs anywhere in the stored order. A third instance in the same article - "It removes the withdrawal that had blocked mineral entry" - went with them. Replaced with the mechanism the Forest Service itself states: the withdrawal "would restrict the BLM from processing or issuing new hardrock prospecting permits and mineral leases".

REMOVED, F-FAIL: "it doesn't repeal the order through ordinary legislation, but declares it null and void as if it had never been issued, which is the CRA's standard language." Two errors. "Null and void" is not the CRA's language and does not occur in 5 U.S.C. 801-808 or in H.J.Res. 140 - both use "shall have no force or effect", which section 802(a) prescribes by defining "joint resolution" to mean ONLY one carrying that formula. And section 801(f) says a voided rule is "treated as though such rule had never taken EFFECT", not as though it had never been issued. Replaced with both statutory texts, quoted.

REMOVED, F-UNSOURCED and U-FLAG: "a protected wilderness area that encompasses more than one million acres and is one of the most visited wilderness areas in the country." No stored source carries a BWCAW acreage, and none supports the visitation superlative. Fetching one was attempted and failed: the Forest Service page for the wilderness now 301-redirects to a generic recreation page carrying no acreage. Both claims removed rather than approximated. Replaced with what 16 U.S.C. 1132 does record - that the BWCAW is a designated wilderness in the Superior National Forest whose authority is Pub. L. 88-577 sec. 3 (1964) and Pub. L. 95-495 sec. 3 (1978).

REMOVED, F-UNSOURCED: "the Lake Superior Chippewa ceded the land to the United States in 1854 but retained treaty rights to hunt, fish, and gather in the ceded area. The BLM's withdrawal factored in those treaty rights in determining the appropriate use of the land." Neither the 1854 treaty terms nor the enumerated hunt/fish/gather rights appear in any stored source, and no stored source says the withdrawal weighed treaty rights in determining appropriate use. The order does state a tribal purpose, in different terms - health, traditional cultural values and subsistence-based lifestyle, and wild rice - and the page now quotes that instead. The 1854 Ceded Territory remains named because both the order and the 2022 assessment notice name it.

REMOVED, F-UNSOURCED: "the proposed Twin Metals Minnesota copper-nickel mine near Ely, Minnesota, which had been progressing through federal permitting for more than a decade before the Biden administration cancelled its mineral leases in 2022". No stored source supports "more than a decade", "near Ely", or the attribution to an administration. FIXED BY SOURCING: the BLM's own 2024 EIS-termination notice sets out the sequence, and the page now follows it - notice of intent June 30, 2020; Forest Service withdrawal application October 2021; "In January 2022, the Department of the Interior cancelled two hardrock mineral leases held by Twin Metals, including lease MNES 1352, because the leases were improperly renewed"; PLO 7917 on January 31, 2023; EIS terminated December 2024. The actor is the Department of the Interior and the stated reason is improper renewal, neither of which the article had.

REMOVED, U-FLAG: "Twin Metals has been the center of a sustained political dispute between Minnesota mining communities, tribal nations, and environmental advocates over the economic and environmental tradeoffs of sulfide mining in the Boundary Waters watershed." An unattributed characterisation of who is on which side of a live controversy, with no source and no receipt available. Replaced with the Forest Service's own statement of why the withdrawal was sought, which is the sourced version of the same point.

REMOVED and RE-ATTRIBUTED, agency-name-as-inference class: "Public Land Order No. 7917, issued by the BLM in January 2023" and "The BLM framed the withdrawal as..." The order was issued "By virtue of the authority vested in the Secretary of the Interior" and signed by Deb Haaland, Secretary of the Interior; the 2022 assessment notice states flatly that "The Secretary of the Interior is the decision-maker for the requested withdrawal"; and the application was filed not by the BLM but by the USDA Forest Service, which was also the NEPA lead agency, with the BLM "a cooperating agency". The BLM label is not simply wrong - the enacted resolution itself calls the order a rule "submitted by the Bureau of Land Management of the Department of the Interior", which is the capacity in which it reached Congress - so the page now states all four roles rather than collapsing them into one.

REMOVED, F-UNSOURCED legal conclusion: "The CRA applies to 'rules' as defined in the Administrative Procedure Act, which includes BLM land orders issued through the rulemaking process." No stored source says the CRA reaches public land orders, and 5 U.S.C. 804(3) expressly carves "any rule of particular applicability" out of the definition. The claim was also contested on the floor: the Senate record shows a "point of order that the measure is not entitled to expedited procedures under the Congressional Review Act", tabled 51-48. Replaced with the statutory definition, the carve-out, what the order covers, and the record of the objection - with no assertion either way about the answer.

FLAGGED FOR JAMES, NOT CHANGED: the page title and H1, "BLM Mining Ban Reversal: What Congress Did to the Boundary Waters". The order was a withdrawal from mineral and geothermal LEASING, not a mining ban - it expressly left ongoing operations on valid existing rights, non-federal mineral interests and mineral-materials sales untouched - and the body of this refresh now says so at length. Retitling a page Google is indexing is an SEO decision, so it follows the pocket-veto precedent from the veto-cluster batch: flag, do not change. The meta description and og:description WERE corrected, since they were describing the mechanism rather than naming the page.
